Prostate-specific antigen monitoring
Measurement of PSA is the cornerstone of follow-up after local treatment. While PSA thresholds depend on the
local treatment used, PSA recurrence almost always precedes clinical recurrence [1436, 1437]. The key question
is to establish when a PSA rise is clinically significant since not all PSA increases have the same clinical value
(see Section 6.4.2) [994]. No prospective studies are available on the optimal timing for PSA testing and the
impact on oncological outcomes.

interventions.body:
WHAT I FOUND
**radiology_report**: The mpMRI Prostate (3T) showed a PI-RADS 5 lesion in the right peripheral zone, measuring approximately 12 mm. This lesion demonstrated markedly restricted diffusion on DWI (b=1400) and early/intense focal enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences. No extracapsular extension or seminal vesicle invasion was identified. The PSA density was 0.12 ng/mL/mL, and the clinical T stage was cT1c.
**pathology_report**: Biopsy timepoint 1 (Aug 2023) and timepoint 2 (Feb 2025) both revealed adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 3+3 (ISUP grade group 1), characterized by a cribriform pattern and intraductal carcinoma (IDC-P). Perineural invasion was not observed. The histological trajectory was stable.
**previous_notes**: The patient presented in Aug 2023 with a PSA of 2.5 ng/mL. Pathology confirmed Gleason 3+3, ISUP grade group 1, with high-risk features (cribriform pattern, IDC-P). Active surveillance was discussed, and the patient expressed anxiety.
**family_history**: Not recorded.
**psa_trend**: The PSA trajectory shows a rise from 2.5 ng/mL in May 2023 to 4.53 ng/mL in February 2025, with a dip to 1.5 ng/mL in December 2023.
**laboratory_results**: The most recent PSA was 4.5 ng/mL on January 9, 2025. Other labs included a Free PSA of 1.23 ng/mL (27% Free PSA), with normal renal function (eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73m2).

WHAT IS NOT RECORDED
The family history is not recorded.

previous_notes.author: Dr. F. de Boer (GP)
previous_notes.text: Patient presented with incidentally elevated PSA of 2.5 ng/mL. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable. Given the PSA level and age, a transrectal ultrasound-guided systematic biopsy was performed. Pathology returned showing Gleason 3+3, ISUP grade group 1, with noted cribriform pattern and IDC-P. Patient was informed of the findings and the presence of high-risk features. Active surveillance was discussed, but the patient expressed anxiety regarding the high-risk patterns and requested a second opinion on management options. Referred to urology for further evaluation and discussion of treatment pathways.
